title: Sukkot: building
hookLine: even a small sukkah on a balcony counts
tomorrow: who else gets invited to the hut, besides your friends?

lines: A BALCONY THE SIZE OF A PARKING SPACE.
A TABLE IN THE WRONG ROOM.
cards: Apartment life has its own version of this problem. No yard, a balcony the size of a parking space, and a holiday that says: build a hut and live in it for a week. "Ye shall dwell in booths seven days," says Leviticus.
On the fourth floor? The tradition's answer is practical, and kinder than people expect, and it hangs on a story about a man eating with his table in the wrong room.

teach.h: THE RULES ARE ABOUT THE ROOF.
teach.b: A sukkah, the booth of Sukkot, has rules, and the ones that trip people up are about the roof, not the size.

The roof is cut branches or other plant material, called schach, laid loose: more shade than sun, but never a solid roof. The Mishnah says a sukkah built under a tree, or inside a house, doesn't count.
So the balcony question is one question: is there open sky above? If another balcony hangs over yours, that's the problem, not the square feet. And how small?
The Mishnah tells of elders from the two schools, Shammai's and Hillel's, visiting a man named Yochanan ben HaHoranit.

teach.h: A MAN WITH HIS TABLE INDOORS.
teach.b: They found him with his head and most of his body in the sukkah, and his table inside the house.
Hillel's school remembered the elders saying nothing. Shammai's school remembered them saying: if that's your habit, you've never kept the commandment.
The law generally follows the school of Hillel, and a little booth, enough for your head, most of you, and a meal, can count. Why a hut at all?
Leviticus gives the reason: "that your generations may know that I made the children of Israel to dwell in booths, when I brought them out of the land of Egypt."
A flimsy roof with sky showing through: a week of remembering that home was once a shelter on the road.

how: During Sukkot, Jews who keep it build a sukkah in a yard, on a balcony or at a synagogue, roof it with branches or bamboo mats, and eat meals in it for the week; some sleep in it too.

o: the spring feast of unleavened bread
a fast day for the fallen Temple
booths: the festival of living in huts

games.q: building a sukkah — tap the pairs.
p: the roof of cut plant material
his table was inside the house
Israel lived in them out of Egypt

s: a sukkah has to be big enough for a dinner party
a small one can count; the law generally follows the school of Hillel.
a sukkah needs open sky above its roof
the Mishnah says one under a tree or inside a house doesn't count.
the roof should be solid enough to keep out rain
it's loose plant material: more shade than sun, never a real roof.

games.q: your friend has a fourth-floor balcony, with another balcony right above it. she wants to build a sukkah there. what's the problem?
o: there's no open sky above it.
a sukkah has to stand on the ground.
games.why: size isn't the issue; the Mishnah rules out a sukkah under a roof or a tree. it needs sky.

practice: For the sit, look up. If there's a window, find the sky in it; if not, the ceiling will do. Ask the sukkah question: what's over my head, and how much of it do I really need?
Then bring to mind the smallest shelter you'd be glad to eat a meal in, with someone you love across a little table.

wordCard.voice: Sukkot: booths. The autumn festival of living in huts under an open roof, where small counts.

orig.note: Hebrew: a booth or hut; Sukkot is the plural, booths.

carryVoice: Hold on to this one: a small hut is enough. Sky above, a little table, someone across it.
